summary: Specifies cryptographic algorithms based on Key Agreement Mechanism 3 (KAM3) for the Mutual user authentication method for HTTP. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: The specific math recipes used by the mutual login scheme.

subtitle: Algorithms using discrete-logarithm and elliptic-curve groups for HTTP mutual authentication.

tldr.problem: RFC 8120 defines the mutual authentication protocol for HTTP but leaves the specific cryptographic algorithms to separate specifications. Implementations need concrete algorithm definitions.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies four authentication algorithms based on ISO Key Agreement Mechanism 3 (KAM3), an augmented password-authenticated key exchange (augmented PAKE) technique. Two use discrete-logarithm groups (2048-bit and 4096-bit) and two use elliptic curves (P-256 and P-521).
tldr.outcome: Implementers have standardized, secure algorithms they can use with the Mutual authentication protocol. The algorithms provide authenticated key exchange and session secret generation resistant to offline password attacks.

today: RFC 8121 specifies Experimental algorithms for HTTP mutual authentication. These algorithms provide the cryptographic foundation for RFC 8120. While cryptographically sound, deployment of mutual authentication for HTTP remains limited, with most web systems continuing to use TLS with simpler authentication schemes.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithms Overview
sections.content:
RFC 8121 specifies cryptographic algorithms for the Mutual authentication protocol defined in RFC 8120. The algorithms are based on ISO/IEC 11770-4 Key Agreement Mechanism 3 (KAM3), a well-studied augmented password-authenticated key exchange (augmented PAKE) technique.

An augmented PAKE scheme allows two parties to authenticate using a shared password while deriving a strong session secret. The password never appears in transmitted messages. The server stores an 'augmented' form of the password (J(pi)) rather than the password itself, improving security if the server is compromised.

This document defines four concrete algorithms: iso-kam3-dl-2048-sha256, iso-kam3-dl-4096-sha512, iso-kam3-ec-p256-sha256, and iso-kam3-ec-p521-sha512. The discrete-logarithm algorithms use MODP groups from RFC 3526. The elliptic-curve algorithms use NIST curves P-256 and P-521.
sections.eli5: These algorithms teach computers how to do the secret handshake. They are proven safe designs that experts have studied. You can choose a smaller, faster one or a bigger, stronger one depending on your needs.

sections.title: Algorithm Specifications
sections.content:
All four algorithms in this family use the same general structure, differing only in the underlying mathematical group and hash function.

Discrete-Logarithm Algorithms: The 2048-bit algorithm (iso-kam3-dl-2048-sha256) uses a 2048-bit MODP group with SHA-256 hashing. The 4096-bit algorithm (iso-kam3-dl-4096-sha512) uses a 4096-bit MODP group with SHA-512 hashing. In discrete-logarithm settings, the client sends K_c1 = g^(S_c1) mod q, where S_c1 is a random secret. The server computes K_s1 = (J(pi) * K_c1^(t_1))^(S_s1) mod q using a hash-derived value t_1 and a random secret S_s1. Both sides then compute the shared secret z using these values and their secrets.

Elliptic-Curve Algorithms: The P-256 algorithm (iso-kam3-ec-p256-sha256) uses the NIST P-256 curve with SHA-256. The P-521 algorithm (iso-kam3-ec-p521-sha512) uses the NIST P-521 curve with SHA-512. In elliptic-curve settings, operations use point multiplication instead of exponentiation. K_c1 represents a point on the curve, K_s1 represents another point, and both sides compute a shared point z using elliptic-curve arithmetic.

All algorithms use a hash iteration count (nIterPi) of 16384 for key derivation. The key-exchange values are encoded as base64 (for discrete-logarithm) or hexadecimal (for elliptic-curve) numbers.
sections.eli5: There are four versions. Two use big numbers (2048 or 4096 bits), two use curves (P-256 or P-521). Each has a matching hash function. They all do the same job; they just use different math.

sections.title: Cryptographic Operations and Security
sections.content:
The key exchange follows this general pattern: The client generates a random value S_c1 and computes K_c1. The server fetches the augmented password J(pi) for the user and generates a random value S_s1. The server computes K_s1 using J(pi), K_c1, and S_s1.

Both sides independently compute a shared secret z. The client computes z from K_s1, its secret S_c1, its password pi, and hash-derived values. The server computes z from K_c1, its secret S_s1, the password pi, and hash-derived values. When both parties used the same password, their z values match.

Verification values (VK_c and VK_s) are derived from the shared secret z, the exchanged values K_c1 and K_s1, and additional context. The client sends VK_c to prove it computed the correct secret. The server responds with VK_s to prove the same. If either verification fails, the authentication is rejected.

Security considerations include: preventing timing attacks by normalizing computation times; cryptographically secure random number generation for S_c1 and S_s1; and the server must only send VK_s after receiving a correct VK_c to prevent offline password attacks.
sections.eli5: The client picks a random number and sends a computed value. The server picks a random number and sends a computed value. Both sides use their secrets plus the password to compute the same shared secret. They exchange proof numbers to verify they both got the same secret.

sections.title: Implementation Security and Deployment
sections.content:
Implementations must take several security precautions. All random numbers (S_c1 and S_s1) must be cryptographically secure to prevent guessing attacks. To prevent timing-based side-channel attacks, computation times for numerical operations must be normalized and made independent of the actual values being computed.

The server must enforce the cryptographic requirement that VK_s (the server's verification value) is only sent after receiving a correct VK_c from the client. Sending VK_s before verification would enable offline password attacks.

Invalid K_s1 values should be rejected rather than retried, as they likely indicate systematic failure or a compromised augmented credential J(pi) rather than random bad luck. The domain parameters must satisfy specific conditions: for discrete-logarithm settings, the prime q must be a safe prime and r the order of the subgroup generated by g. For elliptic curves, r must be prime.

When integrating these algorithms with other protocols, the verification steps between VK_c and VK_s (as defined in RFC 8120) must be carefully considered to prevent mixing values from different key exchanges.
sections.eli5: Programmers must be careful about randomness, timing, and only sending the server's proof after the client proves itself. They must reject suspicious values and make sure the math parameters are valid.
